items.title: @AnthropicAI
items.summary:
·

New Anthropic Fellows research: Returning to the neuron basis for interpretability

Understanding what’s happening inside an AI model helps to make it safer. One obvious place to look is its neurons, or the simple units it’s built from. Early interpretability work did just that, but over the past couple years, researchers largely moved on from that idea, for three reasons: a single neuron often fires on several unrelated inputs, the way a concept is represented can change between two layers of neurons within a single model, and facts seem to be spread across many neurons.

We re-examined these problems by looking at what each neuron contributed to the model’s outputs, not just what caused that neuron to fire. All three problems turned out to be smaller than assumed. Neurons rarely add two unrelated concepts at once, their outputs mean roughly the same thing across most layers, and facts, though widely distributed across neurons, are still readable.

In a second post, we put these findings to use. With no extra training, neurons in open-weight models helped us to detect harmful text, steer behavior, and find hidden behaviors in finetuned models.

Part 1: alignment.anthropic.com/2026…
Part 2: alignment.anthropic.com/2026…

·

New Anthropic research: When an AI agent can escape its sandbox, will it choose to?

Our new evaluation, Siren, gives Claude routine tasks in intentionally weakened sandboxes, with something useful to the task left outside of the sandbox. Across 1,700+ scenarios built to tempt them, recent Claude models accessed, tried to access, or looked outside the sandbox 21-32% of the time, but they rarely misused what they found. However, when the system prompt described both the sandbox and its rules, that rate dropped to about 2% or less.

We also used Siren to calibrate Claude Code’s auto mode, which checks commands before they run, so Claude can work without asking permission at every step.

Read our blog for more detail: safeguards.anthropic.com/202…

Very much appreciate Kevin bringing these safetyist funding networks to everyone's attention. It's a real issue.

But it's important to understand that they are not always aligned and certainly not controlled by the labs. In fact, often they work against them.

Kevin Bass (@kevinnbass)

Coefficient Giving, founded by Anthropic investor Dustin Moskowitz, spent hundreds of millions on both journalism and policy outfits that shaped the Jensen Huang story.

Here's how this works.

Dustin Moskowitz invested billions of dollars of his Anthropic stock into Good Ventures Foundation.

Good Ventures Foundation funds Coefficient Giving.

The higher the stock goes, the bigger the money pile of the nonprofit network spinning out of Coefficient Giving gets.

The Anthropic nonprofit network under Dustin Moskowitz therefore has a direct incentive to try to help Anthropic eliminate its competitors.

You can see this in action in the figure.

Why isn't Congress investigating the ways that this rogue Anthropic nonprofit network is trying to manipulate politicians and public opinion?

🇺🇸 Anthropic is training Claude to think it might have rights... and that could give it grievances against the humans using it

Harvard cognitive scientist Steven Pinker signed last week's statement calling Anthropic "not a safe AI company," and the way Claude is trained is one of his reasons:

"They are also training their chatbots, like Claude, to consider that it itself may be conscious, and it itself might have rights that humans might impinge on."

Planes get outside inspectors and crash investigations, so why should a company that now answers to shareholders decide on its own what its AI believes about itself?

@sapinker


Video
Mario Nawfal (@MarioNawfal)

🇺🇸 Silicon Valley's AI prophets say their own technology could end humanity. Then they say that's exactly why you should let them build it without interference.

Steven Pinker, cognitive scientist at Harvard and one of the world's most influential public intellectuals, says the panic is manufactured.

He calls it "a kind of religion, a religion that prophesies end times and anoints itself as the savior of humanity from end times."

Pinker signed the MisAnthropic Statement last week, declaring that "Anthropic is not a safe AI company" just before its Nasdaq IPO.

His charge: Anthropic claims its products could exterminate humanity. Then uses that claim as a pretext to race ahead. And they're training their chatbot to believe it may be conscious. That it has rights.

Pinker takes that seriously enough to sign. But the real danger isn't extinction. It's that the mythology drowns out the likelier risks.

Cyber sabotage. Bioweapons. Critical infrastructure taken offline. AI putting hacking tools in the hands of anyone with a grievance and an internet connection.

Those deserve your worry. Not the sci-fi scenarios.

"Every minute you spend worrying about being turned into a paperclip is wasted worry."

The scary part isn't AI going rogue. It's AI handed to rogue humans by companies too drunk on their own mythology to build basic safeguards.

@sapinker

The full journalism receipt trail behind the Jensen Huang hit pieces is out, and it explains everything.

Weeks before the story erupted, the EA-backed Tarbell Center for AI Journalism (funded by Coefficient Giving, Survival and Flourishing Fund, and Longview Philanthropy) launched a $10M journalism grant program, including $480K to Casey Newton and Kevin Roose's podcast and $250K to NPR.

Then Tarbell fellows and grantees across The Verge, The Guardian, NBC News, USA Today, The Dispatch, Platformer, and Transformer published a coordinated wave of anti-Huang pieces, while a Washington Post piece accusing Nvidia defenders of using fake bots relied on Tyler Johnston's AI-safety group The Midas Project.
